title: King's Indian, Classical: Black seals the centre and storms the king

difficulty.label: KID player who meets the classical Nf3/Be2 setup

objective.summary: You chose the King's Indian: concede the centre now to attack the king later. Against the classical setup, play the committal sequence in the right order — castle, ...e5, ...Nc6 inviting d5, then reroute and release ...f5 — knowing that every move signs you deeper into the race.

planClasses.label: Invite d5, then storm with ...f5-f4 and ...g5
planClasses.description: The main line's bargain: ...Nc6 provokes d5, the centre locks, and the kingside pawn storm becomes Black's whole game. In this pack it is the spine itself — Ne7, Nd7, ...f5 — with White's queenside race as the clock you play against.

planClasses.label: Trade the centre and play on the long diagonal
planClasses.description: The other King's Indian: ...exd4 keeps the g7 bishop's diagonal open and plays against e4 with pieces. In this pack it exists as the classified door at the 7.O-O decision — choosing it means a different pack's middlegame.

planClasses.label: Delay the commitment (...Nbd7 setups)
planClasses.description: Keep ...c6, ...exd4 and ...a5 all available one move longer. Its cost is the same as every postponement in a race: the storm needs the knight on e7 headed for g6 or f5 eventually, and d7 is not on the way.

annotations: Castle before ...e5: with the king on g8 the e5 push cannot be met by a dxe5/Qxd8 trick that strands your king in the centre.
The classical announcement: White will castle short and race you on the queenside instead of storming your king.
The King's Indian's move. You strike at d4 from a position of deliberate cramp; White must now hold, trade, or advance the centre, and each answer defines a different variation you should recognize.
White keeps the tension. This is YOUR fork in the repertoire: ...Nc6 invites d5 and the race; ...exd4 keeps the diagonal open; ...Nbd7 postpones. The pack's spine takes the main road.
Attack d4 with a piece that is happy to be hit: you WANT d5. When it comes, the knight re-routes to e7 and the pawn chain tells both players where to attack.
The centre closes. From here the position is a race with the finish lines on opposite wings: White queues c5 and the c-file, you queue ...f5-f4 and ...g5.
The only retreat that keeps the storm: from e7 the knight supports ...f5 and can reroute to g6.

White unblocks the f-pawn for f3 and heads the knight for d3, where it pushes the c5 break. Your f6 knight must now clear the way for ...f5 — and which square it chooses is the pack's central decision.
The traditional square: the knight eyes c5 to blunt White's break before rejoining the attack. Its cost is real — the c8 bishop waits behind it.
White reinforces e4 so the coming ...f5 can be met without concessions. Both storms are now fully queued.
The release. From this tabiya the races run on rails: ...f4, ...g5-g4 against c5 and the c-file. Play on and count tempi — the side that spends one on defence usually finishes second.

The modern square: the knight keeps d7 free for the bishop's sake and covers c7 against the queenside invasion, and ...f5 comes just as fast. A different division of defensive labour, not a different plan.

checkpoints.label: 7.O-O — choose your King's Indian before the centre chooses for you
9.Ne1 — pick the f6 knight's retreat square
...f5 — both storms are queued; the race begins
You are past the authored line

deviations.note: 6...c5 steers for Benoni structures after d5: a legitimate repertoire fork that trades the ...e5 chain war for queenside counterplay against the d5 wedge. A different family, not an error.

6...Bg4 pins the knight that guards d4 before committing the centre. It spends the c8 bishop — the piece the main line keeps for the kingside attack — to make ...exd4 and ...Nc6 bite harder. Play it out and see which army you would rather attack with.
7...exd4 is the keep-the-diagonal plan made concrete: after Nxd4 the g7 bishop stares at a real target and the game is about e4, not about pawn storms. The classified door for the second plan class.

7...Nbd7 postpones the choice: ...c6, ...exd4 and ...a5 all stay available. Against the classical race its cost is a tempo of ambiguity — the e7-g6 reroute that powers ...f5 is not on this knight's map.

8...Na5 hits c4 instead of retreating to e7. The question it must answer is where the knight goes when b3 comes and the storm needs it back home. Stated as a question because nothing in this repo has checked the answer — play both and compare.

feedbackClaims.text: At the 1400/1600/1800 rating bands (Lichess blitz+rapid, 2024-01 through 2026-07), the position after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 was reached 5,353,956 times and scores 47.4% for Black against 48.0% for White — the fight you chose is close to even at your level, and 3.Nc3 (77.5%) is overwhelmingly what you will face.

Black's committal order is castle, then ...e5, then ...Nc6, then the reroute: each move is safe because the previous one prepared it, while playing them out of order hands White free forks like the dxe5/Qxd8 tricks against an uncastled king.
Once d5 closes the centre, defensive moves are race moves lost: the side that first spends a tempo answering the other wing usually attacks second from then on.
